solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Divers grab jobs with me – will we take a drop or two in local?

definitions.text: will we take a drop or two in local?
definitions.note: the answer speaks in the first person plural: the drinks themselves ask the question

indicators.note: 'divers' is the old word for various, so the letters come in assorted order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
taken as written, joining the fodder

explanation.surface: Deep-sea divers grabbing work, then asking whether they might pop down to the pub for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divers' looks like people in wetsuits but is the anagram signal. A Jägerbomb is a shot of Jägermeister dropped into a glass of energy drink, so 'a drop' is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: Jägerbombs are the drinks taken 'in local', a local being a neighbourhood pub, and each involves dropping a shot.

clue.text: Rating that’s a wind-up for unhappy motorist?

blocks.note: an ordinary sailor in the navy, not a score
the tool wound up to lift a car with a flat tyre, not a tease

explanation.walkthrough: A rating is an ordinary sailor, and Jack (as in Jack Tar) is the traditional name for one. The second sense is the car jack, wound up to lift a car with a flat tyre.
explanation.definitionFit: A jack is a sailor, and a jack is what a motorist with a puncture winds up to raise the car.

clue.text: Wheeling or dealing for a branched chandelier?

indicators.note: letters set wheeling spin round into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Someone haggling or wheeling and dealing to get hold of an ornate chandelier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wheeling or dealing' reads as the stock phrase 'wheeling and dealing', which hides that 'wheeling' is the anagram signal and 'or dealing' the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A girandole is a branched candlestick or chandelier, often mirrored.

clue.text: Novel about knight, upright type

blocks.note: the French word for a novel, whose medieval ancestors were tales of chivalry
the printer's ordinary upright letters, as opposed to italic

explanation.surface: A reader describing a novel whose hero is a knight in shining armour.
explanation.walkthrough: A roman is a novel (as in roman à clef), and the medieval romances that gave it the name were tales of knights. Roman type is the ordinary upright typeface, as opposed to italic.
explanation.definitionFit: A roman is a novel or verse romance of chivalry; roman is also the name for upright, non-italic type.

clue.text: This may offer choice of fruit or veg

definitions.text: This may offer choice of fruit

blocks.note: taken as written
chard is a leafy vegetable

explanation.surface: A greengrocer's stall offering a choice between fruit and vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit or veg' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops at 'fruit' and the wordplay is just 'or veg'.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: a plot of fruit trees lets you pick apples, pears or plums, a choice of fruit in the literal sense.

clue.text: Decrepit cars from ’98 catch up

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'up' sends the letters from the bottom back to the top

blocks.note: in Britain an S-reg plate marked a car first registered in 1998
nab = catch

explanation.surface: Old cars dating from 1998 struggling to keep up with modern traffic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cars' does double work: 'Decrepit cars' is the definition, while 'from ’98' alone gives S-REG. UK number plates used a year letter then, and S meant a car registered from August 1998.
explanation.definitionFit: Banger is British slang for a battered old car (it is also a sausage and a firework).

clue.text: Let me think whether to review cashier

indicators.note: to review is to look back over, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: er is the sound of someone pausing to think
if = whether

explanation.surface: A manager wondering aloud whether to review a bank cashier's performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cashier' looks like a noun for a bank clerk, but it is the verb meaning to dismiss from service.
explanation.definitionFit: To cashier someone is to dismiss them, especially from the armed forces, which is to fire them.

clue.text: Devoted followers that Raducanu has now secured?

definitions.note: here the whole body of Muslims
read as 1 SLAM: one Grand Slam title

blocks.note: a community of the faithful, not fans
Emma Raducanu won the 2021 US Open, one Grand Slam title, written with the numeral 1 as a letter

explanation.surface: A tennis fan remarking on the loyal supporters Emma Raducanu has won over.
explanation.walkthrough: Emma Raducanu is the British tennis player who won the 2021 US Open, one Grand Slam title: I SLAM. 'Secured' suggests she won over fans, not a title.
explanation.definitionFit: Islam can mean the community of Muslims, the faithful who follow the religion devotedly.

clue.text: Head of Science perhaps has Group T rebelling about compositions

indicators.note: a rebellion is a revolt, a turning over, and 'about' turns the pair round

blocks.note: the head of Science is the letter S, which is spelt ES
say = perhaps, for instance
a set is a group
te is the seventh note in sol-fa, written T

explanation.surface: A science teacher learning that a class, Group T, is revolting over their essays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of Science' is not a teacher: it is the letter S, spelt out as a word (ES). Likewise T is the sol-fa note TE.
explanation.definitionFit: Essayettes are short essays, which are compositions.

clue.text: From after ascent, aunt’s become queasy in jet

indicators.note: in a down clue, letters that ascend are read bottom to top
a queasy stomach churns, so the letters are churned

blocks.note: of = from, as in 'a man of Kent'
anagram fodder
taken as written

explanation.surface: An aunt feeling airsick on a plane just after take-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jet' and 'ascent' suggest an aircraft, but the jet is a jet of water.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym once 'jet' is read as a spout of water rather than an aircraft.

clue.text: Cowboy clamoured, refusing duel, shot in bar?

indicators.note: refusing the duel means leaving those letters out
a cowboy job is a botched one, so the letters are botched

blocks.note: the starting word
these letters leave, giving CAMOR

explanation.surface: A Wild West saloon scene: a cowboy shouting, refusing a duel, gets shot in the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: The saloon picture makes 'shot in bar' a gunshot; the question mark signals the other sense, a shot in bar billiards or any cue game.
explanation.definitionFit: A carom is a cannon in billiards, a shot where the cue ball hits two other balls.

clue.text: Pets might, quite a lot

blocks.note: might and can both express possibility
oodles = a great deal

explanation.surface: A comment that pets may be capable of quite a lot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pets' reads as animals, but it is the verb: to pet is to kiss and cuddle.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who canoodles pets, that is kisses and cuddles amorously.

clue.text: Romantic meeting with one novice, say, before flood

blocks.note: Roman numeral one
a novice is, for example, a trainee nun
a date is a romantic meeting

explanation.surface: A novice's romantic meeting before the flood, which sounds like a tale from a convent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novice, say' asks for an example of a novice, and the classic one is a novice nun.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to cover with water, and both stretch to swamping someone with letters or work.

clue.text: Indefinite number heading close to me? I’ll object

definitions.note: the answer is a person; the definition is what that person says

blocks.note: n is the mathematician's unspecified number
In My Back Yard is right close to me

explanation.surface: Someone saying they will object to anything built close to them.
explanation.walkthrough: NIMBY stands for Not In My Back Yard: N heading IMBY, the back yard being close to me. The definition is the nimby's own catchphrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A nimby objects to developments near their own home, so 'I'll object' is exactly their line.

clue.text: Chemical decomposition of cacti about which great papers may be written

indicators.note: decomposition breaks the letters down and reforms them
the great papers are written around the broken-down cacti

blocks.note: ace = great
anagram fodder, becoming TICAC
ID = identity papers

explanation.surface: A botanist's study of how cacti decay chemically, the kind of subject that earns learned papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great papers' reads as scholarly articles about the chemistry; split in two, the words are a pair of stock abbreviations that wrap around the broken-down cacti.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the answer is the compound that gives vinegar its sourness, one chemical among many.

clue.text: Late filing by me may produce one with kisses on

definitions.text: Late filing by me may produce one
definitions.note: the setter filing late produces a CROSS ED, an angry editor

blocks.clueFragment: Late filing by me may produce one
blocks.note: 'me' is the setter; a puzzle filed late leaves the editor angry, and the answer splits into those two words
kisses at the foot of a letter are written as Xs

explanation.surface: A setter admitting that sending in a crossword late may produce a letter with kisses on it.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as CROSS ED: if the setter ('me') files a puzzle late, the editor will be cross. The kisses are the crosses, X, on a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: marked with the X that stands for a kiss, and, split as CROSS ED, an angry editor.

clue.text: Diamond steeplechaser with odds fixed on run

blocks.note: SP = starting price, the odds at the start of a race
Arkle was a famous Irish steeplechaser, three-time Cheltenham Gold Cup winner
R = run, as on a cricket scorecard

explanation.surface: Racing talk about a star steeplechaser with its odds rigged for the race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fixed' suggests race-fixing, but it only places SP on the front. Arkle was a legendary Irish steeplechase horse of the 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang sense: jewellers' and crooks' slang names gems, especially diamonds, for the way they glitter.

clue.text: Hardy girl cuddling Mae West – that’ll press the sheets!

indicators.note: the girl's arms go around Mae
in an across clue, going west means reading right to left

blocks.note: Tess of the d'Urbervilles, Thomas Hardy's heroine
taken as written

explanation.surface: Tess hugging the film star Mae West, with a racy exclamation about bedsheets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mae West' is one name in the surface, but only MAE is fodder; 'West' is the reversal signal. The sheets are sheet metal, not bedding.
explanation.definitionFit: A seamset is a tool used to press down and flatten seams in sheet metal.

clue.text: Where in Whitechapel you’ll find 5 go through the roof?

definitions.note: sky rocket is rhyming slang for pocket, where you might keep sausages or old cars (5-down BANGERS)

blocks.note: Cockney rhyming slang for pocket, where you might stash 5-down
to soar, as prices do

explanation.surface: Asking where in Whitechapel the bangers will shoot up through the roof, like fireworks going off.
explanation.walkthrough: Whitechapel is in the East End of London, home of Cockney rhyming slang, where 'sky rocket' means pocket. 5 refers to 5-down, BANGERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the rhyming-slang word for a pocket, and the verb for soaring suddenly, as fireworks and prices do.

clue.text: Blasted heath on which 1 Downs journey

indicators.note: the heath is blasted apart and its letters scattered

blocks.note: anagram fodder
1-down is JACK, and J is the abbreviation for a jack in cards; two of them give JJ

explanation.surface: The blasted heath from Macbeth, pictured as the route of some travellers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blasted heath' is a famous phrase from Macbeth, so 'blasted' seems part of the scenery rather than the anagram signal. The cross-reference gives jacks, each J.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hajj is the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca, a journey.

clue.text: Lively member has the ego to crack anti-Freudian

indicators.note: cracking into Jung puts the letters inside him

blocks.note: Carl Jung broke with Freud
Member of Parliament
ego is Latin for I

explanation.surface: A lively politician whose ego is big enough to break a psychoanalyst, borrowing Freud's own word 'ego'.
explanation.walkthrough: The Freudian vocabulary makes 'ego' look psychological; here it is just Latin for I.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal sense: a place full of noise and dancing is said to be buzzing in exactly this way.

clue.text: It may display extremes of virility, essential with trim

definitions.text: It may display extremes of virility, essential with trim

indicators.note: trimming cuts the end off the word

blocks.note: the two ends of VIRILITY are V and Y
key = essential, trimmed of its last letter

explanation.surface: A macho display of manliness, with a neat trim as an essential finishing touch.
explanation.walkthrough: The extremes of virility are V and Y, with the word AND taken literally between them. Read whole, the clue describes the answer: a beard shows off manliness and needs regular trimming.
explanation.definitionFit: The short pointed beard named after the painter Van Dyck is a display of virility that must be kept neatly trimmed.

clue.text: Producer of art, never more surreal, no parts drawn

indicators.note: drawn out, like teeth, so those letters are removed
surreal means bizarrely distorted, so the letters are distorted

blocks.note: the starting letters
the letters N and O are taken out, leaving EVERMRE

explanation.surface: An art critic declaring an artist will never be so surreal again, with no parts of the picture drawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawn' looks like art vocabulary alongside 'surreal', but it means pulled out: the parts of NO are extracted.
explanation.definitionFit: Johannes Vermeer was the Dutch painter of Girl with a Pearl Earring, a producer of art.

clue.text: Excellent try

blocks.note: first-rate, the way elite troops or a top marksman are described
an attempt, as in 'have a go'

explanation.walkthrough: Crack as an adjective means first-rate (crack troops); to have a crack at something is to have a try.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: an informal adjective for first-rate, and an informal noun for an attempt.

clue.text: In circulation, Financial Times, Time and Post

indicators.note: circulating letters move round, so the last one comes to the front

blocks.note: the pink British newspaper is known as the FT
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A list of newspapers in circulation: the Financial Times, Time magazine and the Post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Post' looks like another newspaper title; it is the Latin prefix post-, meaning after. FTERA cycles its final A round to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latin prefix used as a word: post- in post-war and postgraduate means later than.

clue.text: Will he be too quick for Aussies to observe ball?

definitions.text: Will he be too quick for Aussies
definitions.note: he is the answer, a person

blocks.note: to mark = to observe, take note of
a wood is a ball in the game of bowls

explanation.surface: A cricket fan wondering whether a bowler will be too fast for the Australians to see the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Wood is an England fast bowler, one of the quickest in the world. In lawn bowls, the balls are called woods.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Wood's pace is his weapon against Australia in the Ashes cricket series.

clue.text: I’m having fun with large disc

blocks.note: 'whee!' is the cry of someone having fun
L = large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: Someone enjoying themselves throwing a big frisbee or spinning a record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm having fun' is not a statement to paraphrase but a sound: the exclamation WHEE.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: many are solid round plates, such as a potter's or a cheese, so disc stands in fairly.

clue.text: Chief caught king out

indicators.note: the king is sent out of the word

blocks.note: to catch what someone says is to hear it
R = rex, king; this letter leaves

explanation.surface: A cricket scene where the captain has caught the batsman called King out.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture makes 'caught' a dismissal; it means heard, as in 'I didn't catch that'.
explanation.definitionFit: Chief and head both mean the person in charge.

clue.text: Critic, at her ineptest, collars Duchess

indicators.note: the words grip the answer inside them like a collar

blocks.note: critiC AT HER INEptest

explanation.surface: A critic, at their most clumsy, collaring a duchess to interview her.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across four words, starting with the last letter of 'Critic'.
explanation.definitionFit: Catherine was Duchess of Cambridge before becoming Princess of Wales.

clue.text: Maybe wino will leave area for base woman

indicators.note: the area letter leaves and the base letter takes its place

blocks.note: an alkie is an alcoholic, a wino being one example
A = area; this letter goes
e is the base of natural logarithms

explanation.surface: A drunk being moved on from one spot to a military base, perhaps for a base woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' is not low or a camp: e is the mathematical constant used as the base of natural logarithms. Elkie Brooks is a British singer.
explanation.definitionFit: Elkie is a woman's name, as borne by the singer Elkie Brooks.

clue.text: Talk Radio is holding back secret

indicators.note: the words hold the answer inside them
the held letters read backwards

blocks.note: taLK RADio read backwards

explanation.surface: A talk radio station holding back a secret from its listeners.
explanation.walkthrough: Talk Radio is a real British station, which makes the name look like one unit; the answer runs backwards across its two words.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep something dark is to keep it secret.

clue.text: As time allows in a good day, before and after hours

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase for an adjective: age-related means governed by how much time has passed

indicators.note: the hours words sit in the day

blocks.note: taken as written
G = good
ere is old-fashioned for before
after hours is late
D = day

explanation.surface: Someone fitting things in as time allows during a good day, before and after working hours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before and after hours' reads as one span of the working day, but it is two separate pieces; the 'day' they sit in supplies only its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Something age-related changes as time allows it, with the passing years.
